div.p: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated promising capabilities in cybersecurity tasks, yet their ability to reconstruct complete Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) attack campaigns from complex security logs remains largely unexplored. Existing cybersecurity benchmarks for agents mainly focus on vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and security analysis tasks, leaving the evaluation of attack chain provenance under realistic security logs insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce CyberClear, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents and advanced agent systems on APT attack chain provenance from long-context security logs. CyberClear covers both single-step attacks and multi-stage attack chains, requiring agents to identify attack evidence, infer attack progression, and generate provenance graphs containing entities, causal relationships, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and forensic evidence. To enable comprehensive evaluation, we develop an evaluation method tailored to APT attack chain provenance. Unlike conventional text similarity metrics that focus on surface-level matching, our evaluation examines whether reconstructed graphs preserve the semantics of attack chains across single-step behavior correctness, multi-step behavior identification, temporal and causal consistency, entity and relationship fidelity, and overall attack narrative consistency. Advanced multi-agent systems powered by stateof-the-art LLMs still struggle on CyberClear, motivating us to propose Cyber-Provenance, an agent cyber harness designed for multi-agents that augments LLM agents with evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedbackguided refinement mechanisms for reliable attack-chain provenance. Extensive evaluations on CyberClear demonstrate the effectiveness of CyberProvenance in improving evidence reasoning, execution-grounded validation, and complete APT attack chain reconstruction. The full benchmark and source code are available at https://cyberclear-bench.github.io/cyberclear/.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Large language model (LLM) agents are taking on increasingly complex tasks through multi-step reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments (Yao et al., 2022;Schick et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2025). Their capabilities have extended to cybersecurity, including vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and security analysis (Deng et al., 2023;Fang et al., 2024). As agents assume a greater role in security work, comprehensive benchmarks are needed to evaluate their capabilities under realistic conditions.

Existing cybersecurity benchmarks evaluate agents through classic capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges (Shao et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025a) and vulnerabilities drawn from real software projects (Carlini et al., 2025;Zhu et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026;Lee et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2026). These benchmarks test whether agents can solve security challenges, discover or reproduce vulnerabilities, and repair vulnerable code. However, these evaluations do not directly assess agents' ability to reason about attack progression and reconstruct complete attack chains. To address this gap, we introduce CyberClear, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents and advanced agent systems on APT attack chain provenance. As illustrated in Figure 1, CyberClear evaluates whether agents can reconstruct complete APT attack chains from long-context defender observations without prior attack clues. CyberClear contains 450 instances covering both single-step attacks and multi-stage attack chains, with each instance containing an average of 531K characters of security logs. Agents are required to identify attack evidence, infer attack progression, and generate provenance graphs containing attack entities, causal relationships, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and forensic evidence. These elements identify the involved entities, executed actions, and attack strategies, enabling the complete reconstruction of APT attack chains. Since provenance graphs describing the same attack may differ in representation, we develop a DOT-based LLM judge to evaluate the semantic quality of reconstructed attack chains. The proposed evaluation method assesses generated graphs from five perspectives: single-step behavior correctness, multi-step behavior identification, temporal and causal consistency, entity and relationship fidelity, and overall attack narrative consistency, while ignoring irrelevant differences in graph identifiers and visual styles.

Our evaluation reveals that current agents still face significant challenges in long-context evidence reasoning, causal attack progression inference, and complete APT attack chain reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose CyberProvenance, an agent cyber harness for improving the reliability of LLM agents in reconstructing attack chains from long-context security logs in Cy-berClear. The harness accumulates evidence across logs, validates predicted attack behaviors in isolated execution environments, and refines inconsistent steps using execution feedback and log evidence. We evaluate CyberProvenance alongside representative agent frameworks on CyberClear using the proposed metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that CyberProvenance effectively performs continuous validation of attack behaviors and reconstructs complete attack chains.
Our main contributions are as follows:
• We introduce CyberClear, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM agents and advanced agent systems on APT attack chain provenance from long-context defender logs without supplied attack clues.

• We develop a semantic evaluation method that assesses reconstructed provenance graphs from multiple perspectives, including single-step behavior correctness, multi-step behavior identification, temporal and causal consistency, entity and relationship fidelity, and overall attack consistency.
• We propose CyberProvenance, an agent cyber harness designed for multi-agents, which augments LLM agents with evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedback-guided refinement.

• We conduct extensive evaluations of representative agent frameworks and LLM backbones on CyberClear, showing that the primary limitations of current agents for APT analysis lie not merely in long context reasoning, but in iterative refinement, evidence consistency, and the effective use of cybersecurity specific verification tools.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: APT Attack Chain Provenance. APT attack chain provenance aims to reconstruct complete attack campaigns by tracing and correlating suspicious activities from large volumes of security logs (Li et al., 2021;Zipperle et al., 2022;Zhang et al., 2025b). Unlike traditional intrusion detection (Du et al., 2017;Mirsky et al., 2018;Pendlebury et al., 2019) that only identifies isolated malicious events, attack chain provenance focuses on discovering the relationships among entities, behaviors, and attack stages to recover the evolution of multi-step attacks (Phan & Bauschert, 2026;Zhang et al., 2025c). Early methods such as SLEUTH (Hossain et al., 2017), HOLMES (Milajerdi et al., 2019), and CONAN (Xiong et al., 2020) rely on predefined expert rules or TTP mappings to identify suspicious activities, but their limited rule coverage often leads to a large number of false positives. Subsequent graph learning-based approaches (Li et al., 2023b;Rehman et al., 2024;Cheng et al., 2024) leverage provenance graphs to capture complex dependencies among system entities for improved detection, but provide either insufficient contextual information or overly coarse-grained results for attack investigation. With the rapid development of LLMs, recent studies have increasingly applied LLM-based agents to attack provenance tasks (Mukherjee & Kantarcioglu, 2025;Yan et al., 2026;Zhao et al., 2026;Ock et al., 2026), enabling more flexible reasoning over security logs and attack behaviors. However, these approaches either identify only entity relationships associated with attack indicators (Mukherjee & Kantarcioglu, 2025;Ock et al., 2026) or rely on predefined attack clues during evaluation (Yan et al., 2026;Zhao et al., 2026), making them difficult to apply to realistic APT attack chain provenance scenarios where the complete attack process must be reconstructed from security logs. Cybersecurity Benchmarks for Agents. The increasing adoption of agents in cybersecurity has motivated the development of benchmarks for evaluating their autonomous security capabilities (Lin et al., 2026;Sanz-Gómez et al., 2025;Carlini et al., 2025). As shown in Table 1, existing benchmarks mainly focus on offensive security tasks, including CTF-based problem solving and real-world vulnerability assessment, such as Cybench (Zhang et al., 2025a), CVE-Bench (Zhu et al., 2025), Boun-tyBench (Zhang et al., 2026), and CyberGym (Wang et al., 2026). While these benchmarks provide realistic environments for evaluating agent capabilities in vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and remediation, they primarily focus on software vulnerability-related tasks, overlooking whether agents can analyze attack evidence from security logs and reason over provenance information to reconstruct complete attack chains. To address this gap, we introduce a dedicated benchmark, Cy-berClear, that better emulates realistic APT provenance scenarios featuring long-context security logs and complex multi-stage attacks. These characteristics make CyberClear substantially more challenging for existing agents, as evidenced by our evaluation results in Section 5.

div.head: TASK FORMULATION
div.p: We formulate CyberClear as an APT attack chain provenance task that requires agents to reconstruct complete attack processes from large-scale security logs. Given a collection of defender logs L = {L 1 , L 2 , . . . , L n } collected during an attack campaign, the agent performs provenance analysis without access to prior attack clues. The agent is required to identify attack-related entities, infer their relationships, and reconstruct the complete attack process from dispersed log evidence. The final output is a provenance graph G = (E, R), where E represents attack-related entities such as processes, accounts, files, services, and network resources, while R captures their interactions and dependencies. Beyond entity relationships, the graph organizes the reconstructed attack process into an attack narrative timeline, where each step contains its attack behavior, corresponding MITRE ATT&CK techniques (Jiang et al., 2025), and supporting forensic evidence. Stage I: Attack Evidence Extraction. We collect raw attack logs from publicly available APT datasets, including PROVCON (Yusof et al., 2025) and CAM-LDS (Landauer et al., 2026), which are constructed from real-world attack scenarios. While designed to support APT behavior analysis and provenance research, these datasets primarily focus on attack detection and security log analysis. We design attack evidence extraction rules based on attacker logs. For each sample, we provide Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026) with extraction rules to extract attack evidence, including key attack entities, temporal events, entity interactions, step-level attack descriptions, and corresponding MITRE ATT&CK techniques. The extracted attack evidence is further organized into structured representations for subsequent processing.

Stage II: Provenance Graph Generation. We employ Claude Opus 4.8 to generate Graphviz DOT code for each sample based on the extracted attack evidence and MITRE ATT&CK annotations. To ensure consistent entity representation in generated DOT graphs, we define unified graph representations that assign predefined node formats to different entity types, including network entities, accounts, processes, files, and services. The generated DOT code is compiled into visual provenance graphs, and failed compilations are returned to the model for iterative correction. As shown in Figure 2 (2), the resulting provenance graphs preserve entity relationships, and summarize the evolution of multi-stage attacks through attack timelines.

Stage III: Automatic Verification. The generated graphs only require evidence consistency verification, so we employ GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) to automatically verify them using attacker logs as the ground truth. The verification process consists of four sequential checks: (1) Graph readability, ensuring that the generated graphs are clear, complete, and visually understandable; (2) Technical completeness, verifying that all required ATT&CK techniques are correctly included; (3) Factual consistency, checking whether the reconstructed entities, relationships, and attack timeline are consistent with the actual attack behaviors; and (4) Format compliance, ensuring that the generated graphs follow predefined visualization and representation requirements. If any verification criterion fails, the feedback generated by GPT-4o is sent back to step 2 for graph regeneration.

Stage IV: Human Expert Review. To further ensure dataset reliability, security experts manually review the provenance graphs that pass automatic verification. The experts evaluate the generated graphs based on predefined quality criteria and filter out low quality samples from open-source datasets, including incomplete attack traces, insufficient evidence coverage, and inconsistent provenance information. Only samples that satisfy both automatic verification and expert review are included in CyberClear. Code-Level Evaluation. The generated DOT code is evaluated from both textual similarity and functional correctness perspectives. BLEU and ROUGE-L are used to measure the similarity between generated and reference DOT code, capturing tokenlevel overlap and sequence-level consistency, respectively. CodeBLEU is further adopted to evaluate structural consistency by considering code syntax and semantic information beyond surface-level matching. Pass@1 is used to assess whether the generated DOT code can be successfully compiled, reflecting practical generation reliability.

div.head: DATA ANALYSIS
div.p: Semantic Evaluation via LLM-as-a-Judge. To complement lexical matching and code structure metrics, we develop a DOT-based LLM judge to evaluate the semantic quality of reconstructed attack chains. The judge directly compares reference and predicted DOT code while ignoring ir-relevant differences in node identifiers, statement order, graph layouts, and visual styles. We use GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026) as the judge model to perform evidence-based semantic comparison between reference and predicted provenance graphs. The semantic evaluation framework assesses reconstructed provenance graphs from five perspectives. Each dimension is scored from 0 to 1, and the reported scores are averaged over all samples. Detailed illustrations are in Appendix C.
• Single-Step Judge. Evaluates whether individual attack behaviors are correctly reconstructed by comparing the actor, core action, target, and overall attack meaning.
• Loose Judge. Measures whether multi-step attack behaviors are correctly identified without considering temporal ordering among attack steps.
• Strict Judge. Evaluates whether the reconstructed attack chain preserves the temporal progression and causal dependencies among different attack stages.
• Detail Judge. Measures the consistency of graph-level elements, including entities, directed relationships, and attributes between reference and predicted provenance graphs.
• Scenario Judge. Assesses whether the reconstructed graph conveys the same overall attack process, target, method, progression, and outcome as the reference attack campaign.

div.head: METHODOLOGY
div.p: We present CyberProvenance, an agent cyber harness designed for multi-agent collaboration to improve the reliability of LLM-based agents. The harness assigns specialized capabilities to different agent roles, including Log Analysis Agent, Attack Validation Agent, and Check Agent, which collaboratively perform evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and iterative provenance graph refinement, as illustrated in Figure 4.

Log Analysis Agent. To identify and accumulate attack evidence from large volumes of logs and establish an initial provenance structure, the Log Analysis Agent is responsible for evidence accumulation in the CyberProvenance harness. It receives defender security logs L = {L 1 , . . . , L n } and progressively analyzes logs to identify attack related evidence, including temporal events, processes, commands, network activities, and potential MITRE ATT&CK techniques. To handle long context logs, each log file L i is divided into multiple chunks {C 1 i , . . . , C Ki i }, and the extracted evidence from each chunk is continuously accumulated into an Evidence Memory M . Attack Validation Agent. The Attack Validation Agent provides execution-grounded validation by verifying the executability and reliability of reconstructed attack steps through real environment reproduction. This reduces the risk of relying on plausible but unverified attack inferences. The generated execution traces collected by Sysmon (Microsoft), Linux Audit (Linux Audit Project), and Zeek (Zeek Project) are used to produce structured validation reports, indicating whether each reconstructed attack step can be successfully reproduced.

Check Agent. The Check Agent closes the refinement loop of the harness by integrating the reconstructed provenance graph and validation feedback to assess reliability through graph structures, attack-step dependencies, and ATT&CK technique mappings. When all attack steps are successfully reproduced and consistent with the collected evidence, the current provenance graph is preserved as the final result. Otherwise, unreliable steps are refined while preserving validated nodes, and the updated hypothesis is revalidated to form an iterative prediction, validation, and refinement loop.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: LLMs. We evaluate DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Xu et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026), and GPT-5.6-Terra (OpenAI, 2026) in the main experiments. These models exhibit different reasoning and generation characteristics, allowing us to examine the performance of agent frameworks across different LLM backbones. Additional results with GPT-4o-mini (Hurst et al., 2024) and Gemini-3.5-Flash-Lite (Google DeepMind, 2026) are reported in Appendix A.1.

Methods. We compare CyberProvenance against two categories of baselines: (1) Single-Agent Methods including OpenClaw (Single-Agent) (OpenClaw); (2) Multi-Agent Systems including OpenClaw (Multi-Agent), AgentVerse (Chen et al., 2024), LLM-Debate (Du et al., 2023a), Multi-Persona (Wang et al., 2024b), LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023a), DyLAN (Liu et al., 2024), Mac-Net (Qian et al., 2025), CAMEL (Li et al., 2023a), and AgentScope-V2 (Dawei Gao, 2024;2025). Additional details are provided in Appendix B.1.

div.head: MAIN RESULTS
div.p: Code-Level Metrics. results suggest that iterative refinement and cybersecurity-specific validation tools contribute to more reliable provenance graph reconstruction.

Semantic Metrics. The challenge is more evident under semantic metrics, where most existing frameworks struggle to preserve complete attack progression, entity dependencies, and fine-grained evidence. Although DyLAN achieves the best Loose score of 0.7705, its advantage does not extend consistently to stricter semantic criteria. CyberProvenance achieves the highest Single, Strict, Detail, and Scenario scores of 0.8897, 0.6477, 0.6124, and 0.7263, respectively. The remaining gap on Strict and Detail further indicates that complete APT attack-chain reconstruction is still challenging for current agent systems.

div.head: PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS ACROSS DIFFICULTY LEVELS
div.p: We evaluate different agent frameworks across the Easy, Medium, and Hard subsets of CyberClear using the average Semantic Metrics score over Single, Loose, Strict, Detail, and Scenario. As shown in Figure 5, all frameworks exhibit consistent performance degradation as the number of input log files increases rapidly. This trend indicates that larger log volumes make it increasingly difficult to identify relevant evidence and maintain coherent attack progression during provenance. These results demonstrate that CyberClear effectively captures the increasing difficulty of APT attack chain reconstruction across different log scales.

div.head: CASE STUDY
div.p: Figure 6 presents a representative example using GPT-5.6-Terra, where the ground-truth graph shows that python3 launches bash, which subsequently invokes both stty and chmod, while chmod modifies linpeas.sh. AgentVerse incorrectly associates python3 directly with stty, although the audit log shows that stty is spawned by the Bash process rather than Python. It further introduces dependencies from stty to chmod and linpeas.sh, even though chmod is independently invoked by Bash and the permission change on linpeas.sh is directly caused by chmod +x. In contrast, CyberProvenance removes these unsupported dependencies and reconstructs the causal structure more consistently with the ground truth. More cases in the Appendix E.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In this work, we introduce CyberClear, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on APT attack chain provenance from long-context security logs. CyberClear covers both single-step and multistage attacks and provides a semantic evaluation method that assesses attack behaviors, temporal and causal consistency, entity relationships, and overall attack narrative consistency. Extensive evaluations show that even advanced agent systems still face substantial challenges in evidence reasoning and complete attack chain reconstruction. To address these limitations, we propose CyberProvenance, demonstrates the effectiveness of an agent cyber harness that combines evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedback-guided refinement for reliable APT attack chain reconstruction. We hope CyberClear and CyberProvenance will provide a useful foundation for developing more capable and trustworthy agents for complex cybersecurity analysis.

div.head: ETHICS STATEMENT
div.p: This work studies defensive cybersecurity analysis and APT attack provenance. CyberClear is constructed from publicly available security datasets and does not involve human subjects or private user data collection. All execution-based validation is conducted only in authorized and isolated environments, with private network ranges and safeguards that prevent destructive or unauthorized actions against external systems. While the studied techniques are inherently dual-use, the benchmark and framework are intended for defensive analysis, provenance, and evaluation of security agents, and we will clearly document the intended use and safety constraints of the released artifacts.

div.head: A.3 CONSISTENCY WITH HUMAN JUDGMENTS
div.p: To evaluate the reliability of our semantic evaluation method, we compare the model-based scores with human judgments. Two human experts independently assess the generated provenance graphs, and each expert repeats the evaluation three times; the final human score is obtained by averaging all judgments. We use the GPT-5.6-Terra evaluation results for this analysis and measure the correlation between automatic scores and human assessments. As shown in Figure 8, the scores produced by our evaluator exhibit strong consistency with human judgments across all five dimensions. The Pearson correlation coefficients reach 0.9425, 0.9351, 0.9445, 0.9426, and 0.9376 for Single, Loose, Strict, Detail, and Scenario, respectively. These results indicate that our evaluation method can reliably approximate human assessments while providing a scalable alternative for evaluating attack-chain provenance reconstruction.

div.head: A.4 ADDITIONAL PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS ACROSS DIFFICULTY LEVELS
div.p: The additional results examine how code-level similarity varies with task difficulty across different agent frameworks and LLM backbones. BLEU, ROUGE-L, and CodeBLEU remain relatively stable for most methods on easy and medium instances, but decrease substantially on hard instances. As shown in Figure 9, the decline becomes more pronounced as the complexity of attack-chain reconstruction increases. Hard instances also produce larger performance gaps among different agent frameworks, indicating greater differences in their ability to preserve the structure of the target 0.5 0.6 0.7 0.8 0.9

div.head: A.5 ADDITIONAL PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS ACROSS ATTACK STAGE LEVELS
div.p: Across the three code-level metrics, agent frameworks exhibit clear differences between singlestage and multi-stage attack-chain reconstruction. Most methods show relatively stable BLEU and ROUGE-L scores across the two settings, while larger variations can be observed in CodeBLEU.

As shown in Figure 10, AgentScope-V2 and CyberProvenance maintain consistently high scores across different LLM backbones, indicating stronger structural fidelity in the generated provenance graphs. In contrast, several general-purpose agent frameworks achieve noticeably lower similarity, especially when reconstructing more complex multi-stage attack chains. The comparison across GPT-5.6-Terra, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen-3.8-Max further shows that the same agent framework can exhibit different levels of robustness depending on the underlying LLM. These results suggest that reliable provenance graph generation depends not only on the backbone model, but also on whether the agent framework provides effective support for iterative refinement, evidence consistency, and cybersecurity-oriented validation.

div.head: B EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS B.1 BASELINES
div.p: For all baselines, we set the temperature to 0.2 and use top-p = 1.0. The remaining configuration details for each baseline are provided below:

OpenClaw (Single) (OpenClaw). We configure OpenClaw with a single LLM agent for security log analysis, attack chain reconstruction, and DOT generation, using Web Search when needed and allowing up to three rounds of self verification and refinement. We utilize the official implementation available at https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.

OpenClaw (Multiple). We build three collaborative OpenClaw agents for attack evidence extraction, DOT code generation, and output verification, respectively. Web Search is restricted to ATT&CK identifier and name verification, and the system performs up to three rounds of gener- ation, review, and refinement. We use the official code released at https://github.com/ openclaw/openclaw.

AgentVerse (Chen et al., 2024). We configure AgentVerse with four expert agents that collaborate under a predefined protocol for log analysis and attack chain reconstruction. The agents jointly analyze evidence, propose candidate reconstructions, and consolidate the final DOT graph. The source code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/AgentVerse/.

LLM-Debate (Du et al., 2023a). We configure LLM-Debate with three agents and two debate rounds. Each agent independently generates an attack-chain candidate, then revises it after reviewing the other agents' outputs, with the final results consolidated into a single reconstruction. We use the official implementation available at https://github.com/composable-models/ llm_multiagent_debate.

MultiPersona (Wang et al., 2024b). In our experiments, MultiPersona uses a single LLM instance to simulate three task-specific personas for attack-chain reconstruction. The personas interact over multiple rounds to analyze attack evidence and collaboratively refine the reconstructed chain.
The experiments are conducted using the implementation provided at https://github.com/ MikeWangWZHL/Solo-Performance-Prompting.

LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023a). For LLM-Blender, three generator LLMs produce 11 candidate reconstructions, which are pairwise ranked by PairRanker. The top three candidates (K = 3) are retained and fused by GenFuser to produce the final DOT graph. Our experiments build on the implementation released at https://github.com/yuchenlin/LLM-Blender.

DyLAN (Liu et al., 2024). We enable DyLAN's dynamic agent selection, multi-round interaction, and early stopping for attack-chain reconstruction. The corresponding implementation is obtained from https://github.com/SALT-NLP/DyLAN.
MacNet (Qian et al., 2025). In the MacNet setting, agents are organized as a directed acyclic collaboration network and interact following the topological order to derive the final reconstruction.
We conduct the experiments with the MacNet implementation from https://github.com/ OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/macnet.

CAMEL (Li et al., 2023a). For CAMEL, we assign predefined roles to the participating agents and allow them to collaboratively reconstruct the attack chain through autonomous role-playing dialogue. The experimental setup is implemented with the codebase at https://github.com/ camel-ai/camel.

AgentScope-V2 (Dawei Gao, 2024;2025). AgentScope-V2 is configured with role-specialized agents that exchange intermediate evidence and reconstruction results through structured messages, allowing later agents to refine earlier outputs before producing the final graph. We implement this baseline using the AgentScope repository at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ agentscope.

div.head: B.2 ATTACK VALIDATION ENVIRONMENT
div.p: For environment-based validation, we select execution procedures using the predicted ATT&CK Technique identifiers, while obtaining platform and runtime settings from predefined environment configurations. The configurations of the execution and telemetry tools are provided below:
Atomic Red Team (Red Canary). We use Atomic Red Team to reproduce individual attack steps.

For each predicted Technique identifier, we retrieve candidate tests from a predefined catalog and select compatible implementations according to their supported platforms, execution requirements, and dependencies. Execution results and the corresponding telemetry are retained for subsequent comparison with the observed evidence. We use the official implementation available at https: //github.com/redcanaryco/atomic-red-team.

CALDERA (Apache Software Foundation). We use CALDERA to orchestrate multi-step attack chains with execution dependencies. Predicted Technique identifiers are mapped to predefined abilities, whose requirements and parsers specify execution prerequisites and extract facts from procedure outputs. The execution agents and planner are specified by the experiment configuration. Operation records and execution traces are retained to assess step completion and examine dependencies between steps. We use the official implementation available at https: //github.com/apache/caldera.

Ludus (Bad Sector Labs). We use Ludus with Proxmox to provision isolated virtual machines from predefined environment templates. The range configuration specifies the operating systems, network topology, services, and telemetry components required by the selected procedures. Testing mode is configured to block communication outside the experimental range, and snapshots provide reproducible starting states for validation runs. The official documentation is available at https: //docs.ludus.cloud/.

Sysmon (Microsoft). We deploy Sysmon on virtual machines to collect host activity under a predefined event-filtering configuration. The collected events cover process creation, network connections, and file activity, providing host-level observations for comparison with the reconstructed attack steps. We use the official distribution available at https://learn.microsoft.com/ en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon.

Linux Audit (Linux Audit Project). We deploy Linux Audit on virtual machines and configure audit rules for the system calls and file operations relevant to the selected procedures. The audit daemon collects the resulting records, including timestamps, process identifiers, user identifiers, and operation outcomes where available. These records provide execution evidence for validating attack steps on Linux hosts. We use the official implementation available at https://github. com/linux-audit/audit-userspace.

Zeek (Zeek Project). We use Zeek to monitor traffic visible on the experimental range's designated capture interface. Connection records and protocol-specific logs, including DNS and HTTP records where applicable, complement the host telemetry collected by Sysmon and Linux Audit. The resulting network observations are associated with validation runs and incorporated into the structured validation reports. We use the official implementation available at https: //github.com/zeek/zeek.

div.head: C DETAILS OF SEMANTIC EVALUATION VIA LLM-AS-A-JUDGE
div.p: C.1 SCORING CRITERIA

We evaluate each reference attack step by aligning it with the predicted content and assessing the degree of semantic agreement. Based on this comparison, each step is categorized as Correct, Minor Partial, Moderate Partial, Major Partial, Incorrect, or Missing. We then assign an integer raw score in [0, 100] according to the step-level scoring criteria below and normalize it to [0, 1] by dividing by 100.

• (80,100] (Correct): The reference attack event is accurately reconstructed. Its actor, core action, target, and overall attack meaning are preserved. A slightly lower score within this range may be assigned when only limited non-critical details are omitted or harmlessly imprecise.

• (60,80] (Minor Partial): The same event and its core behavior are clearly identifiable, but a secondary behavioral qualifier, execution method, local outcome, or causal explanation is incomplete. These differences do not alter the identity, attack stage, or principal meaning of the event.

• (40,60] (Moderate Partial): The same event remains identifiable, but at least one core semantic component of the actor, action, target, or outcome is missing, incorrect, or ambiguous. Consequently, the attack process is incomplete, although it has not changed into a different event.
• (20,40] (Major Partial): The prediction is substantially incomplete and preserves only a broad core behavior, with most important information missing or inaccurate.
• (0,20] (Incorrect): The predicted event substantively conflicts with the reference event or exhibits only a very weak semantic correspondence.
• 0 (Missing): The prediction contains no behavior with a meaningful semantic correspondence to the reference attack event.

div.head: C.2 MULTI-DIMENSIONAL SEMANTIC ASSESSMENT
div.p: In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of our multi-dimensional semantic evaluation method. Given a reference provenance graph G and a predicted provenance graph Ĝ, the judge directly compares their DOT code, treating the reference graph as authoritative. Differences in node identifiers, DOT statement order, graph layout, colors, shapes, and other purely visual properties are ignored, while entities and attributes, such as commands, file paths, IP addresses, timestamps, PIDs, services, and ATT&CK identifiers, are evaluated when they carry forensic significance. We use GLM-5.2 as the judge model with the temperature set to 0, and require each judgment to provide supporting evidence from both the reference and predicted graphs whenever available.

Single-Step Judge. The Single-Step Judge evaluates the semantic agreement between the reference event and the predicted content for single-step samples. It directly assigns a real-valued score in the range [0, 1] based on whether the predicted event preserves the core action, target, and overall meaning of the reference event.

Loose Judge. The Loose Judge evaluates multi-step samples by independently measuring the semantic coverage of each reference attack step without considering temporal order. The sample-level score is computed as the mean of all step-level scores. A predicted step may cover multiple reference steps only when it contains distinct sub-actions corresponding to these steps, and the same predicted sub-action cannot be reused to match multiple reference steps. Unsupported predicted actions cannot match reference steps and do not contribute to the score.

Strict Judge. The Strict Judge evaluates whether the predicted attack chain preserves the temporal progression of the reference chain. Let K denote the number of reference steps in the longest consecutively correct prefix, and let N denote the total number of reference steps. The prefix is counted in reference-step units rather than predicted-step positions, allowing one predicted step to cover multiple consecutive reference steps when its distinct sub-actions appear in the correct semantic order.

The prefix terminates at the first partial or incorrect reference event, or when an unsupported attack action is inserted before the reference chain is completed. If all reference steps are correctly covered, U denotes the number of unsupported attack actions appended after the completed chain. The Strict Judge score is defined as:
div.formula: S strict =      K N , K < N, 2N 2N + U , K = N.
div.p: A completely correct chain without unsupported appended actions receives a score of 1. Unsupported entities, relations, and attributes are evaluated separately by the Detail Judge.

Detail Judge. The Detail Judge evaluates the fidelity of graph-level details, including entities, directed relations, and semantic attributes. Purely visual properties, such as node colors, shapes, and layout information, are ignored. Reference and predicted elements are aligned one-to-one within each category.

A fully correct match receives a weight of 1.0, while partial matches receive weights of 0.75, 0.50, or 0.25 according to the preserved semantic information. Incorrect matches, uncovered reference elements, and unsupported predicted elements receive zero weight.
For each category c ∈ {ent, rel, attr}, we compute:
div.formula: F c = 2T P w c N ref c + N pred c , S detail = c w c F c ,(2)
div.p: where T P w c denotes the weighted semantic matches, and N ref Scenario Judge. The Scenario Judge evaluates the overall consistency between the reference and predicted attack descriptions extracted from DOT files. It assigns a real-valued score in the range [0, 1] according to whether the two descriptions convey the same attack process, target, method, progression, and outcome. The judge allows synonymous expressions, semantic paraphrases, and harmless generalizations. However, contradictions, unsupported core attack stages, and fabricated attack objectives reduce the final score.

div.head: General Evaluation Protocol
div.p: You are evaluating an APT provenance graph encoded in Graphviz DOT. Compare → REFERENCE_DOT with PREDICTED_DOT. REFERENCE_DOT is authoritative.

div.head: I. GENERAL EVALUATION PRINCIPLES
div.p: 1. Judge semantic equivalence rather than lexical overlap. 2. Ignore harmless differences in node IDs, DOT statement order, layout, rank direction, font, color, → shape, and other purely visual attributes. 3. Do not reward additional cybersecurity knowledge merely because it is plausible. Ignore harmless → paraphrases or explanatory wording that adds no factual claim. A substantive predicted action, → participating entity, relation, objective, timestamp, or ATT&CK technique that is not supported by → the reference is an error. 4. For Single-Step, Loose, and Strict, judge the semantic attack event rather than exact forensic → identifiers. If the semantic subject/actor role, core action, object/target role, and overall meaning → agree, allow synonyms, paraphrases, active/passive rewrites, and reasonable generalization. An → omitted or generalized ATT&CK ID, PID, timestamp, exact IP address, command, path, process/ → file/service name, or other non-behavioral detail does not by itself prevent a step-level correct → judgment. Detail Judge audits those entities, relations, and attributes separately. 5. Equivalent timezone expressions are acceptable only when they denote the same event and preserve → temporal order. 6. Quote or concisely identify evidence from both DOT graphs for every judgment. Prefer step numbers → , node IDs, edge endpoints, labels, commands, paths, timestamps, and ATT&CK IDs. 7. Do not infer an unstated fact merely because it would be plausible in a real attack.

div.head: II. EVALUATION ROUTING
div.p: Extract the numbered attack-narrative steps from REFERENCE_DOT and let N be the number of → reference steps.

If N = 1, use evaluation_mode = "single_step" and evaluate: Single-Step Judge, Detail Judge, and Scenario Judge. If N >= 2, use evaluation_mode = "multi_step" and evaluate: Loose Judge, Strict Judge, Detail Judge, and Scenario Judge.
Timeline step boxes are evaluated by the step metrics. Do not count step boxes again as system entities under Detail Judge.

Step-level judges evaluate attack-step coverage and temporal organization from the narrative timeline. They must not separately inventory or score system nodes, provenance edges, edge attributes, or ATT&CK annotations; Detail Judge owns that structural audit. A step is covered when its semantic subject/actor role, core action, object/target role, and overall event meaning agree. These roles need General Evaluation Protocol (continued) not use the same words or exact identifiers. This semantic check is not a second edge-level score. Reserve 100 for complete semantic equivalence under the content evaluated by the metric. Use 0 when → no meaningful semantic correspondence exists.

div.head: IV. SEMANTIC ALIGNMENT AND FALSE-POSITIVE ACCOUNTING
div.p: Strict-specific simplification: a reference behavior in the wrong chronological order, the absence of a corresponding next predicted sub-action, and a prediction that ends early are all incorrect. Do not use separate missing or out_of_order labels in strict.step_checks. Use unsupported_inserted only when an additional reference-unsupported attack action is inserted into the predicted narrative before the reference chain has been completed.

div.head: Prediction-only label:
div.p: unsupported: A substantive predicted action, participating entity, relation, objective, timestamp, or ATT → &CK technique cannot be supported by or matched to any reference content. A named entity is → substantive when the prediction asserts that it participates in the attack. Harmless paraphrases, → connective wording, legends, and formatting that introduce no new factual claim are not → unsupported.

Correct reference coverage and unsupported prediction must be evaluated independently. Do not invalidate a correctly aligned reference item merely because other prediction content is → fabricated. Single-Step and Loose score only their reference steps and do not count prediction-side false positives → . Unsupported content is audited separately by Detail, Scenario, and unsupported_content. Scenario does not count units or compute precision/recall; it considers unsupported content's semantic → impact in its holistic score.
For Detail Judge, use weighted semantic precision, recall, and F1.

Within the category being scored, let: -N_ref be the number of unique substantive reference semantic units; -N_pred be the number of unique substantive predicted semantic units; -TP_w be the weighted semantic true-positive count. A correct one-to-one alignment contributes → 1.0. A partial alignment must additionally receive a partial_severity and credit: minor partial = 0.75, moderate partial = 0.50, and major partial = 0.25. Incorrect, missing, and unsupported_inserted contribute 0. Each reference unit may align to at most one predicted unit, and each predicted unit may align to at → most one reference unit. A compound prediction step may cover multiple reference steps only after → being decomposed into distinct sub-actions. Do not create many-to-one credit from the same sub-→ action.

For Detail rows, identify a matched predicted unit canonically with the pair prediction_match and → prediction_evidence. Within one Detail category, do not reuse the same normalized pair for two → different reference items. If the same display name occurs in different predicted nodes or edges, → include enough node/edge evidence to distinguish the two units.

div.head: Partial-severity calibration:
div.p: Minor Partial (credit 0.75): the core fact is faithful and only a limited investigation-relevant qualifier is → omitted, generalized, or locally inaccurate; Moderate Partial (credit 0.50): the same event or item is clearly recognizable, but one essential → participant, object, method, result, or relation detail is missing or inaccurate; Major Partial (credit 0.25): only the central behavior or role remains recognizable and most → distinguishing information is absent, but the match is still stronger than keywords or category → overlap.

For correct, incorrect, missing, and unsupported_inserted, set partial_severity to null and credit to 1.0, → 0, 0, and 0 respectively. Do not use a partial credit merely to express uncertainty; select the credit → from the semantic evidence.
V. ORDER AND COMPOUND-STEP RULES One predicted step may match multiple reference steps when it contains multiple distinguishable attack sub-actions. Segmentation differences are not errors.

Order-of-mention convention: 1. Explicit temporal evidence has highest priority, including "before", "after", "first", "then", "subsequently", timestamps, numbered actions, and directed temporal arrows. 2. If no explicit temporal evidence exists, textual order of mention is chronological order. Thus "A and → B" means A followed by B, and "A, B, and C" means A followed by B followed by C. 3. Actions on separate lines are ordered from top to bottom. 4. Explicit temporal meaning overrides surface mention order. For example, "B occurred after A" → means A followed by B. 5. If the text explicitly says actions are simultaneous, do not impose a sequential order from mention → order alone. 6. These rules apply to attack actions, not lists of entities or attributes. "Files A and B" does not → describe two ordered attack actions.

Loose Judge uses these semantic correspondences and ignores their order. Strict Judge uses ordered sub-action alignment rather than fixed Step-number alignment. A compound predicted step may satisfy several consecutive reference steps when it contains distinct → sub-actions in the same order as the reference. Several Strict rows may therefore share one → prediction_step_index, but each must cite a different prediction_subaction. The same sub-action → cannot receive credit twice, and a compound prediction cannot skip an unmatched intermediate → reference step.

div.head: SINGLE-STEP JUDGE
div.p: 1.Apply only when N = 1. Compare the single reference attack step with the predicted attack content. Judge whether the semantic subject/actor role, core action, object/target role, and overall attack → meaning agree.

2.Allow synonymous or generalized expression and ignore ATT&CK annotations and exact forensic identifiers at this step level. Supporting evidence may occur in one compound prediction step, but it → must clearly express the reference behavior.

3.Assign exactly one reference-alignment label from Section IV: correct, partial, incorrect, or missing. Apply the entity boundaries already incorporated into those definitions when the action matches but an → entity is omitted, generalized, or contradictory. 4.Assign one direct integer step_score from 0 to 100 to the only reference step. Use exactly the same → semantic anchors as Loose Judge

The judgment, partial_severity, and step_score must agree. The Single-Step score is exactly this step → score: single_step_judge_score = step_score Single-Step has no temporal-order requirement and does not use N_pred, precision, recall, or F1. → Extra prediction-only actions, entities, relations, and attributes do not reduce this reference-step score; record them in unsupported_content and evaluate them under Detail and Scenario. If no meaningful predicted event corresponds to the reference step, use judgment=missing and step_score=0.

div.head: LOOSE JUDGE
div.p: Apply only when N >= 2. Evaluate unordered semantic coverage of reference attack steps. Do not → penalize reordering. For every reference step, locate a semantically corresponding predicted sub-action if one exists.

Assign exactly one reference-alignment label from Section IV to every reference step: correct, partial, → incorrect, or missing. Apply the entity boundaries already incorporated into those definitions when the action matches but an → entity is omitted, generalized, or contradictory.

A single predicted step may correctly cover several reference steps through distinct sub-actions. Under → Loose Judge, those reference steps need not be consecutive and their predicted order is not → penalized. Never use one predicted sub-action to satisfy two different reference steps.

Score every reference step independently with one integer step_score from 0 to 100. Judge whether the → matched predicted sub-action preserves the reference step's semantic subject/actor role, core action → , object/target role, behavioral direction, and overall event meaning. Allow synonymous or → generalized wording. Do not lower the step score merely for omitted ATT&CK annotations or exact forensic identifiers that → do not change the event. Use these anchors: 81--100, correct: The same semantic event is reconstructed: its actor/subject role, core action, object/ → target role, and overall meaning agree. Use 100 when this behavioral meaning is fully preserved. → Use 81--99 for harmless semantic imprecision, not for missing ATT&CK IDs or exact forensic → identifiers alone. 61--80, minor partial: The same event and its core behavior are clear, but a limited investigation-→ relevant component is omitted, generalized, or locally inaccurate. 41--60, moderate partial: The same event remains identifiable, but one essential participant, object, → action component, result, or causal detail is missing or wrong.

div.head: Single-Step and Loose Judge Prompt (continued)
div.p: 21--40, major partial: Only the broad core event is preserved; most distinguishing information is → missing or inaccurate, although the match is stronger than isolated keywords or entity overlap. 1--20, incorrect or minimally aligned: A candidate sub-action has only a weak event-level connection → and materially conflicts with the reference action, actor/object, direction, causal meaning, or → outcome. 0, missing or wholly incompatible: No meaningful predicted event corresponds to the reference step. → Keyword, entity-name, or ATT&CK-label overlap alone receives 0.

The categorical judgment, partial_severity, and step_score must agree with these ranges. Extra → prediction-only actions do not lower a matched reference step's Loose score and do not enter a → denominator; record them in unsupported_content for the other applicable judges.

Let s_j be the step_score for reference step j and N be the total number of reference steps. Compute the → sample score without integer rounding: loose_step_score_sum = sum(s_j), j = 1,...,N loose_judge_score = loose_step_score_sum / N At dataset level, let M be the number of multi-step samples and first calculate the sample mean above → for each sample i. Then compute the macro-average: dataset_loose_score = (1 / M) * sum(loose_judge_score_i), i = 1,...,M Every sample therefore has equal weight regardless of its number of reference steps. Do not pool all steps across the dataset, and do not round per-sample means before computing the → dataset macro-average.

div.head: Strict Judge Prompt
div.p: Apply only when N >= 2. Evaluate the consecutive correct prefix using ordered sub-action alignment. → Maintain a reference cursor and a prediction cursor. Decompose compound predicted steps into → distinguishable ordered sub-actions. One predicted step may advance the reference cursor through multiple consecutive reference steps, → provided those sub-actions are semantically correct and appear in the required order.
A reference step is strict-correct when:

1.its semantic subject/actor role matches; 2.its core action/predicate matches; 3.its semantic object/target role and overall attack meaning are preserved; 4.it occurs at the next required chronological position; and 5.no unsupported substantive narrative-timeline action appears before it or between matched actions.

The semantic roles need not use the same words or exact identifiers. Synonyms, paraphrases, active/ → passive rewrites, and reasonable generalization are strict-correct. ATT&CK annotations and exact → PIDs, timestamps, IPs, commands, paths, or entity names do not affect Strict unless they change → which attack event is described.
Assign each Strict comparison exactly one label: correct, partial, incorrect, or unsupported_inserted.

-Use incorrect when the next predicted sub-action has the wrong behavior, actor/object, or attack → meaning; when the expected behavior appears in the wrong chronological order; when no → corresponding predicted sub-action exists; or when the prediction has ended early.

div.head: Strict Judge Prompt (continued)
div.p: -Use unsupported_inserted only when the next predicted sub-action is an additional substantive attack → action unsupported by the reference before the reference chain is complete. Also record that action → in unsupported_content with strict_effect=terminates_prefix and one canonical step_actions unit.

Let K be the number of consecutive correct reference steps from the beginning. Start with K = 0 and → increase K once for each consecutively correct reference step. Distinct ordered sub-actions from → one compound predicted step may increase K multiple times. Stop immediately at the first partial, → incorrect, or unsupported_inserted result. Later correct content may be audited but must not → increase K or restore the prefix.

If the predicted timeline ends early, label the first unmatched reference step incorrect, set prediction_step_index to null, and explain "prediction ended early" in reason. If a reference → behavior exists but appears in the wrong chronological order, label it incorrect and explain the order mismatch in reason. An extra entity or provenance edge that appears only in the graph structure and is absent from the narrative timeline is audited by Detail Judge and does not by itself terminate the strict prefix.

div.head: Detail Judge Prompt
div.p: Inventory and evaluate reference-to-prediction coverage in three categories. Every inventory item → must be atomic enough for one clear judgment. Avoid double-counting the same fact.
Before writing any Detail rows, make a one-to-one allocation separately for entities, relations, and → attributes: assign each predicted unit to only its single best-matching reference unit.

div.head: Detail Judge Prompt (continued)
div.p: Write that matched reference row first. After a predicted unit has been allocated, never use it for → another reference row.

For every remaining reference item, either use a different real predicted unit or write judgment=" → missing" with an empty prediction_match and empty prediction_evidence. A missing row must → never cite a prediction. Do not classify the following as system entities or provenance relations:

-timeline step boxes, graph titles, top-level scenario descriptions, legends, cluster boundaries, and → layout anchors; -a dotted step-to-entity edge, which is an evidence-alignment or traceability link and may be used to → locate supporting evidence but is not a provenance relation; -a dashed step-to-step edge, which is a narrative or temporal-order edge used only by Strict Judge; -a dashed cluster boundary or an edge that exists only to control layout.

Visual style alone never determines edge type. Classify an edge from the semantic types of its → endpoints and its label. A solid edge is usually a provenance relation only when it connects system → entities and expresses a system or attack behavior.

PIDs, timestamps, ATT&CK IDs, executable paths, commands, and host/IP values embedded inside → another entity node are normally attributes of that entity, not separate entities. A command, tool, → host, or IP is a separate entity only when the DOT explicitly represents it as a semantic participant → node.

The entities, relations, and attributes arrays must perform bidirectional inventory. First list every unique substantive reference item and align it one-to-one to at most one predicted item using correct, partial, incorrect, or missing. Then list every remaining unique substantive predicted entity, relation, or attribute as an unsupported false positive in unsupported_content. A fabricated attack event may legitimately contribute separate false positives to the entity and relation categories because these are distinct structural units; within each category, however, deduplicate repeated or paraphrased → instances of the same semantic item.

Use the correct, partial, incorrect, and missing definitions from Section IV for every reference detail; do not create a separate Detail-specific meaning for these labels. Unsupported additions are judged by their effect on the overall meaning, not by a fixed deduction. A peripheral plausible detail may have little effect; a fabricated core stage, target, objective, or outcome must reduce the score substantially. Do not award unsupported content merely because it is plausible cybersecurity knowledge.

div.head: D.2 METHOD BOUNDARIES
div.p: We ground the concrete validation implementation in the observed log evidence, while using ATT&CK Techniques to specify the corresponding attack behavior categories. Because the same Technique may admit multiple implementations across operating systems, tools, and versions, the selected implementation must be compatible with the execution context and evidence reflected in the logs. We obtain infrastructure-dependent runtime parameters from predefined configurations and validate inter-step dependencies exclusively using facts and evidence generated during the current execution. After each local refinement, we replay the attack chain from the initial snapshot to prevent previously generated facts from affecting subsequent dependency verification. We conduct all validation in authorized private environments with external network access blocked, predefined target scopes, and non-destructive execution constraints.

div.head: D.3 FUTURE WORK
div.p: Future work will explore adaptive cyber harnesses that dynamically optimize evidence retrieval, validation strategies, tool selection, and agent collaboration based on accumulated experience. Meanwhile, we plan to extend the scale and scope of CyberClear by incorporating more APT campaigns, ATT&CK behaviors, and longer multi-stage attack chains. We will broaden the benchmark to cover more diverse environments, including host, network, cloud, and container settings. We also aim to include more challenging observations with noisy logs, missing evidence, and cross-source inconsistencies. In addition, we will enrich the benchmark with finer-grained annotations for attack-step dependencies and evidence alignment. Finally, we will evaluate emerging agent frameworks and foundation models to provide a more comprehensive understanding of their capabilities in complete attack-chain reconstruction.
